title: Multimodal Models
tagline: Vision transformers, contrastive learning, vision–language models, speech and image generation
summary: Language models increasingly see, hear and speak. This course covers vision transformers and contrastive image–text learning, vision–language models, speech recognition and synthesis, audio and spoken-dialogue models, the diffusion and autoregressive models that generate images, and models trained natively on many modalities.
overview: The recipe that made language models — a Transformer trained on vast data with a simple objective — works for images, audio and video once they are turned into sequences of tokens or vectors. Current assistants read documents and screenshots, describe images, transcribe and speak, and generate pictures. This course explains how other modalities are brought into language models, and how models generate images and speech.

Vision transformers treat an image as a sequence of patches; contrastive training on image–text pairs, as in CLIP, places images and captions in one embedding space and enables zero-shot classification. Vision–language models connect such encoders to language models and are tuned on visual instructions and documents. On the audio side, the course covers speech recognition with encoder–decoder models such as Whisper, neural text-to-speech, and models that turn audio into discrete tokens for real-time spoken conversation. Image generation is treated through diffusion and latent diffusion as well as the autoregressive generation of image tokens, and the course ends with natively multimodal models trained from the start on interleaved text, images, audio and video.

Multimodal systems combine components trained on very different data, and many of their failures — misread text in images, objects hallucinated into captions, speech recognition that falters on unfamiliar accents — come from the seams between them. When you study an architecture, follow one input from pixels or samples to tokens, and ask what each conversion keeps and what it loses.
outcomes: Explain how vision transformers turn images into sequences of patch embeddings.
Describe contrastive image–text training, and use a shared embedding space for zero-shot classification and retrieval.
Explain how vision–language models connect image encoders to language models, and how they are instruction-tuned.
Describe speech recognition and text-to-speech systems, from audio features to tokens.
Explain discrete audio tokens and speech-to-speech models for real-time conversation.
Derive the training objective of diffusion models, and compare diffusion with autoregressive image generation.
Compare late-fusion and natively multimodal (early-fusion) architectures.

history.title: Denoising diffusion
history.detail: Ho, Jain and Abbeel trained a network to reverse a gradual noising process and generated high-quality images, building on the diffusion models of Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues (2015).

history.title: The vision transformer
history.detail: Dosovitskiy and colleagues at Google split images into 16×16 patches and showed that a plain Transformer matches convolutional networks when pretrained on enough data.

history.title: CLIP
history.detail: Radford and colleagues at OpenAI trained image and text encoders contrastively on 400 million image–caption pairs, enabling zero-shot image classification.

history.title: DALL·E
history.detail: Ramesh and colleagues generated images from text with a Transformer that predicts image tokens one by one, as a language model predicts words.

history.title: Flamingo
history.detail: Alayrac and colleagues at DeepMind joined a frozen vision encoder to a frozen language model with new cross-attention layers, so that it learns visual tasks from a few examples.

history.title: Latent diffusion
history.detail: Rombach and colleagues ran diffusion in the compressed latent space of an autoencoder, making high-resolution generation affordable; the model was released as Stable Diffusion.

history.title: Whisper
history.detail: Radford and colleagues trained an encoder–decoder Transformer on 680,000 hours of weakly labelled audio, giving robust multilingual speech recognition.

history.title: Visual instruction tuning
history.detail: Liu and colleagues connected a CLIP image encoder to an open language model through a projection layer and tuned it on visual instructions generated with GPT-4 (LLaVA).

history.title: GPT-4o
history.detail: OpenAI released a model trained end to end across text, images and audio that holds spoken conversations with response times close to a person’s.
